league.name: Sunshine Baseball League
league.mission: Sunshine Ballpark's mission is to offer sports programs and educational opportunities that help young people, especially those who are disadvantaged or facing physical, developmental and other challenges, learn critical life lessons.
league.welcome: The non-profit Sunshine Board welcomes all to "protect and enjoy" the ballpark with its turf fields and playground at 1200 Wicklow Drive in Fredericksburg.
league.about: Sunshine Baseball League offers boys and girls ages 8 to 18 the opportunity to play ball from June 1 to mid-August. We serve Fredericksburg and surrounding communities.

house_rules.keywords: little league rules base which rules apply
house_rules.text: For 10U and 13U, Little League game rules (available in the Little League app) apply, except where these house rules say otherwise.

house_rules.keywords: babe ruth rules base which rules apply
house_rules.text: For 18U, Babe Ruth League baseball rules (baberuthleague.org/documents/RulesBaseball.pdf) apply, except where these house rules say otherwise.

house_rules.keywords: bat bats usa usabat wood legal allowed buy
house_rules.text: All 10U and 13U bats must be USA Bats (USABat) or wood bats.

house_rules.keywords: bat bats bbcor drop usa usabat wood legal allowed buy 14u
house_rules.text: All 18U bats must be BBCOR drop-3 or wood. Players age 14 may also use a USA (USABat) drop-5 bat.

house_rules.keywords: cleats spikes shoes sneakers turf footwear metal
house_rules.text: No cleats or spikes are allowed on the artificial turf at Sunshine Ballpark. Sneakers or turf shoes only.

house_rules.keywords: cleats spikes shoes footwear james monroe jmhs gladys west walker grant armstrong
house_rules.text: Cleats and spikes are allowed during 18U games at the James Monroe High School baseball field at Gladys-West Elementary School, Fredericksburg, VA (formerly called Walker-Grant Middle School Armstrong Field).
house_rules.note: Field name updated by the board on 2026-10-24; the house rules document still uses the old name.

house_rules.keywords: gum bubble sunflower seeds gatorade drinks dugout turf food snacks
house_rules.text: No bubble gum or sunflower seeds on the field or in the dugout at Sunshine Ballpark, because gum and seeds are hard to remove from artificial turf. Only clear Gatorade in the dugouts: Gatorade dye damages the turf.

house_rules.keywords: dugout home visitor third base side which
house_rules.text: The third base dugout is the home dugout. Always.

house_rules.keywords: dugout home visitor first base side which
house_rules.text: The first base dugout is the home dugout. Always.

house_rules.keywords: late arrive arrives arrival shows show up absent missing lineup bottom out bat bats batting order
house_rules.text: A player who arrives late is added to the bottom of the lineup, but not until they arrive. If a player is in the lineup and has not shown up, it is an out the first time that spot comes up, and the player is removed from the lineup. If the player then arrives, they are added to the bottom of the lineup on arrival.

house_rules.keywords: lineup batting order continuous everyone bats bench dugout change
house_rules.text: Every player present in the dugout must be in the batting lineup, and the batting order may not change.

house_rules.keywords: defense playing time innings substitution sub free minimum bench field
house_rules.text: Players may move in and out on defense freely. Every player must play at least two innings on defense; they do not have to be consecutive innings.

house_rules.keywords: injured injury hurt leave early ejected ejection removed out penalty
house_rules.text: A player who is injured or must leave a game early is removed from the lineup with no penalty. If a player is ejected, an automatic out is called each time their spot in the lineup comes up.

house_rules.keywords: eight 8 players seven 7 forfeit minimum start short
house_rules.text: Games may start with eight players. If a team drops to seven players during the game, it is a forfeit.

house_rules.keywords: pitch count pitches limit daily maximum rest days
house_rules.text: Pitch counts: 10U may throw 75 pitches a day; 13U may throw 85 pitches a day. Rest for 10U and 13U: 1-20 pitches, 0 days; 21-35, 1 day; 36-50, 2 days; 51-65, 3 days; 66 or more, 4 days.

house_rules.keywords: pitch count pitches limit daily maximum rest days 105
house_rules.text: 18U pitch limit is 105 pitches. Rest: 76-105 pitches, 3 days; 51-75, 2 days; 26-50, 1 day. A pitcher with 25 or fewer pitches needs no rest day and can pitch the next day.
house_rules.note: Board clarification 2026-10-24: 25 pitches or fewer needs no rest.

house_rules.keywords: innings length long time limit six 6 hour
house_rules.text: 10U and 13U games are six innings. No new inning begins after 1 hour 45 minutes. The last inning will be called at the top of the inning no earlier than 1 hour 30 minutes of game play.

house_rules.keywords: innings length long time limit seven 7 hours playoffs
house_rules.text: 18U games are seven innings. No new inning begins after 2 hours 15 minutes; in the playoffs the limit is 2 hours 30 minutes.

house_rules.keywords: mound distance bases feet field size 46 60
house_rules.text: 10U field: 46-foot mound, 60-foot bases.

house_rules.keywords: mound distance bases feet field size 50 70
house_rules.text: 13U field: 50-foot mound, 70-foot bases.

house_rules.keywords: dropped uncaught third strike 3rd run first advance
house_rules.text: 10U: the batter cannot advance on a dropped third strike.

house_rules.keywords: dropped uncaught third strike 3rd run first advance outs occupied
house_rules.text: 13U: on a dropped third strike the batter can run to first with fewer than 2 outs only if first base is unoccupied. With 2 outs, the batter can run to first whether or not first base is occupied.

house_rules.keywords: steal stealing lead leading off home wild pitch passed ball advance bag
house_rules.text: 10U: no leading off; when the pitcher is on the mound the runner must be on the bag. Stealing is allowed at every base except from third to home. No stealing home, and no advancing on a wild pitch, a passed ball, an error on the catcher's routine throw back to the pitcher, or the pitcher dropping the ball on the mound. If the pitcher or catcher tries to put out the runner on third (or any other runner), the runner on third may try to score. Why: a more competitive game, no easy runs, faster pace, and games won by earned runs rather than errors by a young, inexperienced age group.

house_rules.keywords: steal stealing lead leading off home wild pitch passed ball advance bag
house_rules.text: 13U: no leading off; when the pitcher is on the mound the runner must stay on the bag until the ball reaches the plate. Stealing second, third or home, and advancing on wild pitches and passed balls, is allowed after the pitch reaches home plate.

house_rules.keywords: slide sliding headfirst head first dive pickoff
house_rules.text: 10U and 13U: no head-first sliding, except diving back to a base on a pick-off play.

house_rules.keywords: slide sliding headfirst head first contact collision malicious ejection home plate
house_rules.text: 18U: runners may slide head-first into any base. Runners must slide and avoid contact with fielders at the bases and at home plate. Malicious contact is the umpire's judgment and results in immediate ejection.

house_rules.keywords: warm up warmup pitches between innings pace
house_rules.text: 10U and 13U: 5 warm-up pitches (3 if the pitcher has already pitched more than 2 innings). Fewer if players take too long to get out of the dugout.
house_rules.note: Board clarification 2026-10-24: 13U uses the same warm-up rule as 10U and 18U.

house_rules.keywords: warm up warmup pitches between innings pace
house_rules.text: 18U: 5 warm-up pitches (3 if the pitcher has already pitched more than 2 innings). The umpire may reduce warm-up pitches to keep the pace of play.

house_rules.keywords: five 5 run rule runs inning cap limit last inning unlimited
house_rules.text: Five-run rule: each inning ends when a team has scored five runs, except the last inning. Both teams are unlimited in the last inning.

house_rules.keywords: mercy run rule 10 ten runs ahead after innings
house_rules.text: Mercy rule for 10U and 13U: 10 runs after 4 innings, or after 3.5 innings if the home team is winning.

house_rules.keywords: mercy run rule 10 ten runs ahead after innings
house_rules.text: Mercy rule for 18U: 10 runs after 5 innings, or after 4.5 innings if the home team is ahead.

house_rules.keywords: strike zone strikes balls height small short tall umpire
house_rules.text: 10U and 13U strike zone: adjusted reasonably for the player's age and height, at the umpire's discretion.

house_rules.keywords: strike zone strikes balls letters knees umpire
house_rules.text: 18U strike zone: from the letters to the knees and over the plate. Pitchers at 18U should be able to throw strikes.

house_rules.keywords: taunt taunting trash talk remarks sportsmanship ejection ejected suspension warning arguing argue
house_rules.text: Sportsmanship is paramount in the Sunshine Baseball League. No taunting and no remarks directed personally at players on the other team. After one warning, players or coaches who taunt or argue with umpires will be ejected. Any ejection of a player or coach includes a suspension for the next game, which can be appealed to the league executive board.

house_rules.keywords: umpire call question discuss approach argue dispute coach manager between innings
house_rules.text: If a call or rule is in question, the head coach or manager may ask the umpire if they may approach; discussing between innings is strongly recommended. The head umpire decides whether a play or call needs to be discussed during an inning. Only head coaches or managers may discuss calls with umpires.

house_rules.keywords: coaches umpires example kids friendly approachable goals safe life lesson
house_rules.text: All coaches and umpires should be approachable, friendly and nice: we are setting an example for the kids, and that comes first. Coaches, parents and umpires all share the same goals: a safe game and life-lesson learning for the children playing baseball.

house_rules.keywords: parents fans yell yelling booing polite behavior leave ban removed stands
house_rules.text: Parents and fans must be polite and show good sportsmanship. Coaches should calm fans down, never stir them up; doing so is cause for ejection, suspension and possible expulsion from the league. Parents and fans who do not behave may be asked to leave the ballpark, and repeated problems can lead to season-long or permanent bans.

house_rules.keywords: parents coach coaching sidelines dugout volunteer instructions yelling
house_rules.text: Parents do not coach from the sidelines during games. Only players and approved coaches are allowed in the dugouts during games. Parents who want to coach should volunteer as coaches, not undermine the volunteers who do.

house_rules.keywords: pool player players short shorthanded fill borrow extra gamechanger request
house_rules.text: Teams without enough players for a regular-season game can request pool players by emailing sunshinegamechanger@gmail.com. Pool players bat at the bottom of the lineup, may not pitch or catch, wear their own team jersey and hat, and are entered in GameChanger as pool player 1, pool player 2, and so on.

rule_facts.text: Little League baseball pitchers aged 6-8 may throw at most 50 pitches in a day.
Little League baseball pitchers aged 9-10 may throw at most 75 pitches in a day.
Little League baseball pitchers aged 11-12 may throw at most 85 pitches in a day.
Little League baseball pitchers aged 13-16 may throw at most 95 pitches in a day.

A pitcher who hits the daily limit mid at-bat may finish that batter. The appearance ends when the batter reaches base or is put out, or the half-inning or game ends. A new batter can't be started once the limit is reached.
A Little League pitcher may never pitch on three consecutive days, whatever the pitch counts.
When a pitcher crosses a rest-day threshold while facing a batter, a note in Regulation VI decides which threshold sets the rest days.
A player who catches four or more innings in a game can't pitch on that calendar day. One pitch thrown in the fourth inning counts as catching that inning.
A player aged 14 or under who catches three innings or fewer, then throws 21 or more pitches that day, can't go back to catching that day.
The same restriction for 15-16 year olds starts at 31 pitches.
In Little League, a game can be protested over a playing-rule interpretation or the use of an ineligible player. Umpire judgment calls can't be protested.
Calls that rest on the umpire's judgment, such as balls and strikes or safe and out, are not protestable in Little League.

In the regular season, the manager must tell the umpire right away, before the next pitch or play, that the game is under protest. An ineligible-player protest may be made until the umpires leave the field. A written protest goes to the League President within 24 hours.

A league committee decides regular-season protests: the League President, Player Agent, Umpire-in-Chief, and other officers who aren't managers or umpires. If a protest is upheld, play resumes from the exact point of the infraction.

rule_facts.value: verbal to UIC at once; escalates
rule_facts.text: In tournament play, the protest is made verbally to the Umpire-in-Chief at once. It escalates to the Tournament Director or District Administrator, then Regional Headquarters, and finally the International Tournament Committee, whose decision is final. Umpires and tournament officials can't declare a forfeit.

A courtesy runner may run for the pitcher or catcher with two outs. In the regular season this is a local-league option. In tournaments it's allowed for every team. With a continuous batting order, the runner is the player who made the last out.
New for 2026: in tournament play, or whenever a continuous batting order is used, a courtesy runner may be used for the pitcher or catcher before they've met mandatory play.
New for 2026: with a double first base on an uncaught third strike, both the fielder and the runner may use either part of the base.
New for 2026: pine tar is allowed at all levels of Little League baseball and softball, on the handle or grip only.

Obstruction is a fielder without the ball impeding a runner, with or without contact; a fake tag counts. Whether it happened, and how far the runner would have gotten, are the umpire's judgment. Awarding bases to cancel its effect is the rule.
Little League Majors and below require USABat-marked non-wood bats: at most 33 inches long with a 2-5/8 inch barrel. BPF 1.15 bats are banned.
Little League Intermediate (50/70) and Junior allow USABat or BBCOR bats up to 34 inches with a 2-5/8 inch barrel.
Little League Senior requires BBCOR (or one-piece wood) bats up to 36 inches. A bat may weigh no more than 3 ounces less than its length in inches.
An illegal, damaged or altered bat comes out of play. Choke-up aids must be removed, and repeat offenses can lead to ejections. Penalties for batting with an illegal bat are in Rule 6.06(d).

rule_facts.value: age on Aug 31 of the season year
rule_facts.text: Little League baseball league age is the player's age on August 31 of the season year. For 2026, a player born in January 2014 or September 2013 is league age 12.
Challenger uses the same Aug 31 league-age chart as baseball. For 2026, players born before September 2011 are eligible for Senior League Challenger.
The 2027 Little League baseball chart follows the same Aug 31 rule. A player born in September 2014 through August 2015 is league age 12 in 2027.
New for 2026: thumb protectors are allowed in Little League. Choke-knobs and choke-up assists are still banned.

New for 2026: in Intermediate (50/70), Junior and Senior baseball, a pitcher removed from the mound may come back to pitch even if the team still has visits left. Softball got the same clarification for all divisions.
New for 2026: the Umpire-in-Chief no longer has to sign the scorebook for a forfeited game.
In Little League Challenger, a buddy's job is to protect the player from batted and thrown balls and help only as much as that player needs. The help differs for every player.

Players with full mobility field softly hit balls themselves. For players using a walker or wheelchair, the buddy or a teammate fields the ball and hands it over so the player can make the throw. Talk to a player in a wheelchair at eye level.
A Challenger batter first tries to hit a thrown pitch. If that doesn't work, they move to a tee, with the buddy helping the swing if needed and making sure the bat is dropped before running.

rule_facts.value: one base per hit; all stay until last runner scores
rule_facts.text: In Challenger, runners usually move up one base on each hit, with the buddy running alongside. At the end of an inning, everyone stays on the field until the last runner scores.

rule_facts.value: 60 ft bases; 46 ft pitching; 200 ft+ fence
rule_facts.text: Little League baseball Majors and Minors (including Tee Ball, coach and machine pitch) play on 60-foot bases. The pitcher's plate is 46 feet from home, and the fence is at least 200 feet away.
The Little League Majors/Minors mound is a 10-foot circle with the pitching plate 46 feet from the rear point of home plate.

rule_facts.value: 70 ft bases; 50 ft pitching; 200 ft+ fence
rule_facts.text: Little League Intermediate (50/70) uses 70-foot bases, a 50-foot pitching distance and a 12-foot mound circle, with fences 200 feet or more.

rule_facts.value: 90 ft bases (Junior may use 80); 60 ft 6 in; 300 ft+ fence
rule_facts.text: Little League Junior and Senior baseball use 90-foot bases (Junior may use 80) and a 60-foot 6-inch pitching distance from an 18-foot mound circle, with fences 300 feet or more.

rule_facts.value: 50 or 60 ft bases; 46 ft pitching; 165 ft+ fence
rule_facts.text: The Little League Challenger field uses 50- or 60-foot bases, a 46-foot pitching distance and fences at least 165 feet away.

rule_facts.value: 90 ft bases; 60 ft 6 in; 225 ft+ fence
rule_facts.text: The Senior League Challenger field uses 90-foot bases and a 60-foot 6-inch pitching distance, with fences at least 225 feet away.

rule_facts.value: respect officials; don't confront at the field
rule_facts.rule_ref: Sport Parent Code of Conduct, item 15
rule_facts.text: Under Little League's parent code of conduct, parents respect the officials' authority during games. They don't question or confront coaches at the field; they set up a time and place to talk instead.

rule_facts.value: no booing, taunting or profanity toward officials
rule_facts.rule_ref: Sport Parent Code of Conduct, item 6
rule_facts.text: Parents and their guests agree not to boo, taunt or swear at officials, coaches, players or other parents.

rule_facts.value: asked to leave; next game suspension; repeat escalates
rule_facts.text: A parent who behaves improperly at a game or practice can be asked to leave and suspended from the next game. Repeat violations can mean multiple games or the rest of the season.

rule_facts.rule_ref: Sport Parent Code of Conduct, item 4
rule_facts.text: Parents agree to learn the rules of the game and the league's policies.

rule_facts.value: don't coach unless an official coach
rule_facts.rule_ref: Sport Parent Code of Conduct, item 17
rule_facts.text: Parents agree not to coach their own or other children during games and practices unless they're an official team coach.
Little League umpires are volunteers, and there's no official umpire certification. Each league's Umpire-in-Chief trains them, with support from Little League International.

rule_facts.value: manager to umpire on the field first
rule_facts.text: A Little League protest has to start with the manager telling the umpire on the field. Only then does it go to the league's protest committee, and judgment calls won't be considered.

League-age 12 players must be drafted to Majors, Intermediate (50/70) or Junior. A 12-year-old can play Minors only with a waiver approved by the league board and the District Administrator. If approved, the player can't pitch, can't play All-Stars and can't be moved up for the rest of that season.

rule_facts.value: live or attend school within boundaries
rule_facts.text: A Little League player may play for a league if they live within its boundaries or attend a school physically located inside them. Home schools, cyber schools and sports academies don't count as school attendance.

rule_facts.value: one document from each of three groups
rule_facts.text: Residence is proven with one document from each of three groups, such as a driver's license, a government record and a utility bill, dated within the window the league sets. Moving into a league's boundaries just to qualify for tournament play isn't allowed.

rule_facts.value: continued eligibility after a move or boundary change
rule_facts.text: Under Regulation II(d), a player who previously qualified may keep playing in their league after a move, a school change or a boundary change, and so may their siblings. The claim is filed once in a player's career.

rule_facts.value: date; pitches; league age; eligible again on
rule_facts.text: Little League's pitcher tracking form records the game date, pitches thrown, the pitcher's league age and the date they're eligible to pitch again. Manager signatures are a local option.
A standard 46/60 Little League field can also host Intermediate (50/70) by adding 70-foot base anchors and extending the infield dirt. A field used for both should have its fence 200 to 275 feet out.

rule_facts.value: birth record, federal/military record, or in-lieu statement
rule_facts.text: For tournament (All-Star) play, a player's age is proven with an official birth record, a federal or military record, or an in-lieu statement backed by documents from all four groups.

A tournament player qualifies by residence (documents from three groups), by school enrollment inside the boundaries, or under Regulation II. Regulation II covers a player, or their sibling, who has played in the league continuously since league age 7 or younger.

rule_facts.value: school games can count toward tournament participation
rule_facts.rule_ref: Tournament Player Eligibility Condition 2; Regulation IX
rule_facts.text: Teams claiming the school-participation exception for tournament eligibility list each player's school and league games on a supplemental sheet. From Intermediate (50/70) up, special games can also count toward tournament participation.

In 2012, Little League followed the NCAA's BBCOR decertification of several Marucci bats: the CAT5 33-inch, the CAT5 Squared 34-inch, and the Black 33- and 34-inch. They're illegal in Junior, Senior and Big League. The current list lives at USABat and BBCOR.

rule_facts.value: NOCSAE stamp required; add-ons may void certification
rule_facts.text: Little League batting helmets must meet NOCSAE standards and carry the stamp. Adding a face protector such as a C-flap creates an untested model, and the manufacturer may void the certification. Families should get the manufacturer's written confirmation that the helmet stays certified.
Little League's coach-pitch curriculum recommends one coach for no more than four players during drills, so every child gets more reps and attention.

rule_facts.value: use plastic, soft-core or tennis balls first
rule_facts.text: Being afraid of the ball is normal at this age. The curriculum starts batting and fielding drills with plastic balls, soft-core tee balls or tennis balls until players are comfortable.

rule_facts.value: kneel behind L-screen 25-30 ft; move to mound later
rule_facts.text: For batting practice, the coach kneels behind an L-screen about 25 to 30 feet from the plate, so the batter sees the release clearly. Later in the season the coach moves to the mound, still behind the screen.

rule_facts.value: helmet always; bat only when batting
rule_facts.text: Every player wears a helmet in any drill with a bat. Players hold a bat only when it's their turn, and carry it by the barrel to the box.

rule_facts.value: grip and throw > catch > tee > soft toss > live; baserunning throughout
rule_facts.text: The 12-week coach-pitch plan builds in order: four-seam grip and throwing to a target, two-hand catching (below then above the waist), hitting off a tee, soft toss, then pitched balls. Baserunning, fly balls with a drop step and relays come later. The last week is about enjoying the game and reflecting on progress.
The curriculum states the main goal plainly: Little League is about growing well-rounded people, with confidence and a work ethic, not producing outstanding ballplayers.

rule_facts.value: financial hardship never excludes a child
rule_facts.text: Little League says no child may be turned away from playing for financial reasons. Leagues have options to keep it affordable.

Two runners may not occupy the same base. If two runners are touching the same base while the ball is live, the base belongs to the lead (preceding) runner, and the trailing runner is out when tagged.

Exception: if the lead runner was forced to advance because the batter became a runner, the base belongs to the trailing runner. The forced lead runner is out when tagged, or when a fielder holding the ball touches the base that runner was forced to.

A runner is forced to advance only when the batter becomes a runner and every base behind that runner is occupied. A forced runner can be put out by touching the next base with the ball; a runner who is not forced may stay on their base, and must be tagged to be put out when off it.

On a fly ball that is caught, a runner must be touching (tag up on) their base after the catch before advancing. A runner who left early can be put out if the defense tags the runner or the base before the runner gets back (an appeal).
Babe Ruth Baseball 13-16 allows USABat or BBCOR .50 bats with a barrel of at most 2-5/8 inches.
Babe Ruth Baseball 16-18 requires BBCOR .50 bats; one-piece wood is allowed in every division.
New for 2026 in Babe Ruth and Cal Ripken: each extra inning starts with the previous inning's last batter on second base.
Babe Ruth Baseball (13-18) uses 90-foot bases and 60 feet 6 inches to the pitcher's plate.

Babe Ruth League's guidance is to stop play and get to an enclosed building or hard-top car when lightning is seen or thunder is heard. Dugouts and bleachers aren't safe. Wait at least 30 minutes after the storm has passed before resuming.

Two runners may not occupy the same base. If two runners are touching a base while the ball is live, the base belongs to the lead runner and the trailing runner is out when tagged, unless the lead runner was forced to advance; then the base belongs to the trailing runner and the forced lead runner is out when tagged or when the base they were forced to is touched with the ball.

A runner is forced to advance only when the batter becomes a runner and every base behind that runner is occupied. A forced runner can be put out by touching the next base with the ball; a runner who is not forced may stay on their base.

On a caught fly ball, a runner must retouch (tag up on) their base after the catch before advancing. A runner who left early can be put out on appeal if the defense tags the runner or the base before the runner returns.

lessons.title: Win as a team, lose as a team
lessons.principle: No one wins or loses a game alone. Every player, the coaches and the people in the stands are part of the result.
lessons.life_lesson: Families, classrooms and workplaces work the same way: you share the credit and you share the load.

for.player: One at-bat or one error never decides a game by itself. Pick up your teammates the way you want them to pick you up.
for.coach: Talk about results as 'we'. Never single out the player who made the last out or the last error.
for.parent: Celebrate the team first. After a loss, don't let your child carry it alone or put it on a teammate.
for.umpire: The crew works as a team too, and their calls are part of the game, never the reason a team lost.

lessons.title: Everyone makes mistakes: forgive others, own yours
lessons.principle: Players, coaches, parents and umpires are all human, and we all make mistakes. Forgive the mistakes of others, and take responsibility for your own so you can learn from them and grow. We strive to be perfect, but nobody is.
lessons.life_lesson: Owning a mistake and learning from it is a habit that lasts far beyond the diamond.

for.player: Say 'that's on me', then ask what you'd do differently next time. When a teammate makes a mistake, let it go and pick them up.
for.coach: Model it: own your own coaching mistakes out loud, and treat a player's error as a teaching moment, not a punishment.
for.parent: Show your child how to own a mistake without beating themselves up, and never blame the umpire, the coach or a teammate in front of them.
for.umpire: Umpires miss calls too. Owning that calmly earns respect; everyone else should give the same grace.

lessons.title: Believe in your players before they believe in themselves
lessons.principle: Have confidence in your players even when they don't show it, even when their track record says failure. Don't lose that confidence. Feed it to them and they will succeed.
lessons.life_lesson: People rise to the belief others show in them, at school, at work and at home.

for.player: Your coach picked you for this moment because they believe you can do it. Trust your preparation.
for.coach: Give players the chance to step up, including the ones without a great record yet, and tell them you believe in them before the result.
for.parent: Your belief matters most when your child is struggling. Tell them you love watching them play, hit or no hit.

lessons.title: Winning comes from a winning formula
lessons.principle: Winning is fun and feels great, but it doesn't happen without a winning formula: healthy arms, many players who can contribute, and everyone playing their part. Don't put the scoreboard above developing players.
lessons.life_lesson: Long-term success comes from building people and habits, not from chasing one result at any cost.

for.player: Do your job, whatever your role is that day. A team of players doing their part beats one star.
for.coach: Protect arms and build depth: give more pitchers reps in lower-pressure innings so they're ready when you need them. Rest your best arm when the rules or their body say so.
for.parent: Measure the season by how your child grows and how the team plays together, not only by wins.

lessons.title: Big moments aren't scripted
lessons.principle: The moments that matter most aren't planned. They happen because kids are put in situations where they can fail or succeed, and sometimes they succeed through what could have been failure.
lessons.life_lesson: You can't plan for every opportunity, but you can be ready for it and willing to take it.

for.player: Play every pitch to the end and be ready: your moment can come when you least expect it.
for.coach: Put kids in situations where they can fail or succeed. That's where growth and team belief come from.
for.parent: Let your child take on hard moments. The chance to fail is also the chance to shine.

lessons.title: Believe in your teammates, especially when they fail
lessons.principle: Believe in your teammates, especially when they fail. The moment after a mistake is when a teammate needs your belief most.
lessons.life_lesson: Standing by people when they stumble is what makes a team, a family or a group of friends strong.

for.player: After a teammate's error or strikeout, be the first to say 'next one's yours'. Never roll your eyes or turn away.
for.coach: Teach players how to pick each other up, and praise it when you see it, as much as you praise a hit.
for.parent: Cheer for every player on the team, especially the one who's struggling, and teach your child to do the same.

lessons.title: Your value isn't your stat line
lessons.principle: Your value is not determined by your failures or your successes.
lessons.life_lesson: Who you are matters more than any result: a grade, a game or a job outcome doesn't define your worth.

for.player: A strikeout or a home run doesn't change who you are. Show up, compete and be a good teammate.
for.coach: Make sure every player knows their place on the team doesn't depend on today's box score.
for.parent: Love your child the same after an 0-for-4 as after a 3-for-4, and let them see it.
for.umpire: One missed call doesn't define an umpire either.

lessons.title: A game built on failure
lessons.principle: In baseball, succeeding about 30% of the time at the plate can make a Hall of Fame career at the professional level. That's a 70% failure rate. You will not win every competition, and you will not lose every competition, but you will learn and grow through every competition.
lessons.life_lesson: Failing often on the way to success is normal in anything worth doing; what matters is learning from each try.

for.player: Expect to fail more than you succeed at the plate, even when you're good. Judge yourself by your approach and effort, then go again.
for.coach: Help players keep failure in perspective: celebrate good at-bats and hard effort, not just hits.
for.parent: Remind your child that even the best hitters fail most of the time. A tough day is part of the game, not a sign they don't belong.

lessons.title: Today's opponents, tomorrow's teammates
lessons.principle: Your opponents today may be your teammates in the future. Treat them that way, especially after a game. As competitive athletes in the same sport, you are all brothers and sisters.
lessons.life_lesson: Respect for competitors builds the relationships and reputation you carry for the rest of your life.

for.player: Compete hard, then shake hands like you mean it. Congratulate a good play by the other team.
for.coach: Model respect for the other team and its coaches, and expect it of your players in the handshake line.
for.parent: Cheer for good plays by both teams and speak well of opponents in front of your child. The other team's kids are someone's children too.
for.umpire: Treat both teams the same; respect for everyone on the field starts with the crew.

lessons.title: Control the moment
lessons.principle: When a play gets loud and confusing, the adults set the temperature. Umpires stop the play, get together and explain calmly; coaches lower their voices and wait for the explanation.
lessons.life_lesson: In any heated moment, slowing down and getting the facts straight before reacting keeps a mistake from turning into a fight.

for.player: When the umpire calls time, stop and listen. Don't keep running or tagging because someone is yelling.
for.coach: Yelling directions during a confusing play makes it harder for everyone, including your players. Wait for the umpires, then ask calmly what rule applies.
for.parent: Stay in the stands and stay calm. The players take their cue from the adults.
for.umpire: Kill it loudly: 'Time! Dead ball!' with both arms up. Get your partner, agree on what happened and where everyone goes, then explain once to each coach. Don't let the volume change the call: a misapplied rule can be corrected, and a judgment call stands.

lessons.title: Play until you hear 'foul'
lessons.principle: Every batted ball is live until the umpire says otherwise. Players don't decide fair or foul; the umpire does. So run hard and play the ball until you hear 'Foul!' or 'Time!'
lessons.life_lesson: Don't quit on something because you've already decided how it will turn out. Finish the job, and leave the call to the person whose call it is.

for.player: Hit it, drop the bat and run, every time, until you hear 'Foul!'. Fielders: if the ball is in play, make the play.
for.coach: Teach 'run until you hear foul' at practice with rollers that go foul and come back fair. During a play, one short word ('Run!') helps more than a dozen shouted directions.
for.parent: If your player stood and watched, make it a learning moment on the ride home, not a criticism. 'Run until you hear foul' is a rule many players learn the hard way.
for.umpire: Make the fair signal big and immediate: point toward fair territory as soon as the ball is touched or stops in fair territory. Call 'Foul!' loudly with both arms up. Clear signals stop the guessing and the yelling.

lessons.title: Know the situation before the pitch
lessons.principle: Most baserunning mistakes happen before the ball is hit. Before every pitch, a runner should know how many outs there are, which bases are occupied, whether they are forced to run, and what they will do on a ground ball, a fly ball and a line drive.
lessons.life_lesson: Thinking ahead turns panic into a plan. At school, at work and at home, the people who prepare before the moment make better decisions in it.

for.player: Before every pitch, check: how many outs, where are the runners, am I forced? Then decide: ground ball, go or hold; fly ball, tag up or go halfway; line drive, freeze. Then look at your base coach.
for.coach: Make the pre-pitch check a habit out loud: show the outs with your fingers and ask runners 'what do you do on a ground ball?' A baserunning mistake is usually a teaching gap, not a lack of effort.
for.parent: Baserunning is one of the hardest parts of the game to learn. After a mistake, ask 'how many outs were there?' instead of 'why did you run?' and let your player work it out.
for.umpire: Know the outs and the force situation before every pitch too. It's what lets you get the call right when two runners end up on the same base.

lessons.title: Eyes up: trust your base coach
lessons.principle: A runner can't see the whole field, especially when the ball is behind them. The base coach can. Once the ball is in play, the runner's job is to run hard, find the coach early and follow the signal, even when instinct says otherwise.
lessons.life_lesson: No one sees everything alone. Trusting a teammate who has the better view, and being someone others can trust, is how teams, families and workplaces get it right.

for.player: Run hard and find your coach before you reach the base, not after. Arms up means stop, a windmill means go, palms down means slide. Ball in front of you: your eyes help decide. Ball behind you: the coach decides.
for.coach: Use a few big, simple signals, the same ones every time, and practise them in every baserunning drill. Get in position and signal early. If a runner misses a sign, coach it at practice, not in front of everyone.
for.parent: Cheer the hustle and leave 'go' and 'stop' to the base coach. Shouting from the stands gives a runner two voices to follow and makes the decision harder.
for.umpire: Base coaches may signal and shout, but they may not physically help a runner. Watch for a coach touching or holding a runner who is rounding a base.

insights.situation: Hitter strikes out on pitches away / outside
insights.text: Many youth pitchers miss away from the batter on purpose, because they don't want to hit anyone. Moving closer to the plate (crowding it) brings those outside pitches into reach.
insights.why: If you stand too far off the plate, the outer edge, where most youth pitches end up, is out of your reach.
insights.try_this: Before the at-bat, set your feet so the end of the bat covers the far edge of the plate. If the pitcher keeps missing away, inch closer.

insights.situation: Hitter takes close pitches for strikes
insights.text: In youth games the zone is often called generously, roughly chins to shins and line to line, because pitchers are still developing control and umpires keep the game moving. Treat it as a hit zone: if it's close, be ready to swing.
insights.why: Waiting for a perfect pitch at this level usually means watching strike three.
insights.try_this: In practice, call anything chins-to-shins a 'swing pitch' and react to it. Note how the umpire is calling it in the first inning and adjust.

insights.situation: Two strikes in the count
insights.text: With two strikes, protect the zone: widen what you'll swing at, shorten the swing, choke up slightly, and try to put the ball in play or foul off tough pitches.
insights.why: A ball in play can become a hit or an error; a called third strike can't.
insights.try_this: Two-strike rounds in batting practice: start every rep at 0-2, choke up, shorter swing, battle the outer half off a tee or soft toss.

insights.situation: Pregame, or when unsure how the zone is being called
insights.text: Before the game, a coach can politely ask the plate umpire how they're calling the zone (for example, how wide or how low). Players can also learn a lot by watching the first innings.
insights.why: Knowing the zone tells hitters where to stand and what to swing at, and it builds a respectful relationship with the crew.
insights.try_this: At the plate meeting, ask once, briefly and respectfully, then adjust. Never argue balls and strikes during play: they're judgment calls and can't be protested.

insights.situation: A strikeout or mistake that ends a game
insights.text: A strikeout, even one that ends the game, is one at-bat of information. Talk about the process (were you ready, where did you stand, did you protect with two strikes?), not the result.
insights.why: Players who learn from a tough at-bat instead of fearing the next one get better faster and enjoy the game longer.
insights.try_this: Pick one thing to work on (for example, plate coverage or the two-strike approach), practise it this week, and let the rest go.

insights.situation: Right after a tough game
insights.text: On the ride home, let your child speak first. 'I love watching you play' and praise for effort and approach help more than a breakdown of what went wrong.
insights.why: Kids hear critique from a parent differently right after a loss; support keeps the door open for learning later.
insights.try_this: Wait until they bring it up or until a calm time the next day. Leave technique to the coach unless your child asks you.

insights.situation: A parent wants to help with mechanics or playing time
insights.text: Raise concerns with the coach at a time the coach sets, not right after a game, and don't coach from the stands during play.
insights.why: It keeps one voice coaching the player during games and keeps adult conflict away from the kids.
insights.try_this: Ask the coach for a short conversation later in the week, with your player there, and come with a question rather than a complaint.

insights.situation: A player gets down on themselves
insights.text: Focus on what you control: being ready, your approach, effort and how you respond. Hits and wins depend partly on luck; a good at-bat can still be an out.
insights.why: Measuring yourself by things you control builds confidence that lasts through slumps.
insights.try_this: After each at-bat, grade one controllable (Was I ready? Did I swing at my pitch?) instead of the result.

insights.situation: Frustration with a call
insights.text: Umpires make judgment calls, and youth umpires are often volunteers. Adjusting to the zone you're given is a skill; arguing it never changes it.
insights.why: Players copy how adults treat officials, and respect keeps the game running and the crew wanting to come back.
insights.try_this: Model a calm reaction. If a rule (not a judgment) seems misapplied, the head coach can ask calmly at a stoppage.

insights.situation: Planning a season or a week
insights.text: Players improve with reps: up to age 12, aim for about three-quarters practice or deliberate play to one-quarter games; from 12 to 18 roughly two-thirds to one-third.
insights.why: Games give few touches per player; practice gives many.
insights.try_this: Plan more short, active practices with stations rather than adding more games.

insights.situation: Questions about year-round baseball or softball
insights.text: Playing other sports helps young players develop and stay healthy; USA Baseball recommends no single-sport specialization before age 12.
insights.why: Different movements build athleticism and reduce overuse.
insights.try_this: Keep at least one other sport in the year, and take months off from throwing.

insights.situation: Choosing a bat or wondering if it's too heavy
insights.text: Quick check: hold the bat by the handle with one arm straight out to the side for about 20-30 seconds. If the barrel drops or the arm shakes, the bat is probably too heavy.
insights.why: A bat that's too heavy slows the swing and makes it hard to adjust to pitches, which leads to late swings and pulled-off contact.
insights.try_this: Try the hold test and a few dry swings; if the player drops the barrel or is late, go lighter (a bigger drop) or shorter.

insights.situation: Choosing a bat
insights.text: Start with what's legal in the player's league (for example USABat, BBCOR or USSSA marks, or the softball certification), then fit length and weight to the player. Control and bat speed matter more than size.
insights.why: An illegal bat can be removed or penalized; an oversized bat hurts development.
insights.try_this: Check the league's bat rule, use a sizing chart for length, then do the weight check before buying.

insights.situation: Pitcher fatigue or a heavy week of games
insights.text: Follow pitch counts and rest days, don't pitch on three days in a row, avoid catching on non-pitching days, and take time off from throwing each year.
insights.why: Overuse is the main source of youth arm injuries.
insights.try_this: Track pitches every outing and plan the rotation before a tournament weekend.

insights.situation: Batter hits a ball near the line, or isn't sure it's fair
insights.text: Run hard to first on every ball you hit until you hear 'Foul!' or 'Time!' Fair or foul is the umpire's call, not the batter's.
insights.why: A ground ball near the line can roll foul and come back fair. A batter who stops to judge it gives away an out that running would have saved.
insights.try_this: In practice, roll balls down the lines that go foul and come back fair. The batter runs every one; the fielder makes the play; a coach plays umpire and signals fair or calls foul.

insights.situation: Reading a bat's size or comparing bats
insights.text: A bat's drop is its length minus its weight in ounces: a 30-inch bat at -10 weighs 20 ounces. The bigger the drop number, the lighter the bat. Typical ranges: tee ball about -10.5 to -14, coach pitch -9 to -12, fastpitch -8 to -13; high school and college baseball use -3 BBCOR bats.
insights.why: Matching the drop to the player's age and strength keeps the bat light enough to swing with control, and some leagues limit the drop.
insights.try_this: Read the length and drop printed on the bat (for example 29-inch, -10), work out the weight, then check that the league's bat rule allows it before buying.

insights.situation: Buying a bigger bat to grow into
insights.text: Don't buy a bat to grow into. A bat that's too long or too heavy hurts swing mechanics now, and those habits stick. Fit the bat to the player today: height and weight give a starting length, then watch how it swings.
insights.why: Bat speed and control drive good contact; an oversized bat costs both.
insights.try_this: Use the maker's size chart for a starting length, then have the player try a teammate's bat one size up and one size down and compare the swings.

insights.situation: Taking care of a bat
insights.text: Don't roll or shave a bat: it can void the warranty and make the bat illegal. Composite bats need a short break-in at partial power (follow the maker's instructions), and shouldn't be used in cold weather (below about 60 degrees F) or with heavy yellow cage balls. Turn the bat a quarter turn after each swing so wear spreads around the barrel.
insights.why: An altered or damaged bat can be removed from play, and replacing one is expensive.
insights.try_this: Mark the label side and rotate a quarter turn each swing in batting practice; keep composite bats out of cold-weather games and cage machines.

insights.situation: Choosing a softball bat for a league or tournament
insights.text: Softball has several governing bodies (for example USA Softball, USSSA, NSA, ISA and WBSC), and each certifies bats separately. A bat that's legal in one league may not be legal in another.
insights.why: An uncertified bat can be removed from the game or penalized.
insights.try_this: Before buying or before a tournament, find out which body governs it and look the bat up on that body's certified list.

insights.situation: Before each pitch as a runner
insights.text: Most baserunning outs come from not knowing the situation, not from being slow.
insights.why: When you've decided before the pitch, you react instead of think, and you don't freeze or run into an out.
insights.try_this: Every pitch: check the outs (look for your coach's fingers), know whether you're forced, and decide what you'll do on a ground ball, a fly ball and a line drive before the ball is hit.

insights.situation: Coaching first or third base
insights.text: Runners follow what they can see: a few big, consistent signals work better than words.
insights.why: Crowd noise and a runner's own breathing drown out voices; arms don't get lost.
insights.try_this: Pick three signals (both arms up = stop, windmill = go, palms down = slide) and use them in every baserunning drill so they're automatic by game day.

insights.situation: After a baserunning mistake
insights.text: A baserunning mistake usually means the situation was confusing, not that the player wasn't trying.
insights.why: Shame makes players hesitate on the bases; questions help them learn to read the situation.
insights.try_this: On the ride home, ask two questions: how many outs were there, and what did the coach signal? Let your player work out the right play.

insights.situation: Teaching situational baserunning at practice
insights.text: Baserunning sense is learned in game-like reps, not explained once.
insights.why: Players have to see ground balls, fly balls and line drives with runners on to recognize them in a game.
insights.try_this: Situation drill: put runners on base, call out the outs, and hit fungoes (ground ball, fly ball, line drive). Runners react while base coaches signal; after each rep, ask the runner why they ran or held.

situations.name: Dropped third strike, bases loaded, 2 outs
situations.offense: The batter can run because there are two outs, even though first base is occupied. Everyone runs: every runner is forced to move up. Batter: drop the bat and sprint to first right away.
situations.defense: Every base is a force. The simplest out is often for the catcher to pick up the ball and step on home plate, or throw to first. Don't rush into a wild throw: one clean force ends the inning.
situations.common_mistakes: Batter walks back to the dugout thinking it's over; runners stop; catcher tags the batter late or throws wildly instead of taking the sure force at home.

situations.name: Dropped third strike, runner on first, 1 out
situations.offense: With first base occupied and fewer than two outs, the batter is out and can't run, whether or not the catcher holds the pitch. The runner on first is NOT forced; he may try to advance at his own risk.
situations.defense: The batter is already out. Don't throw to first; watch the runner. Keep the ball in front, call 'batter's out' loudly so the infield knows, and only throw if the runner is trying to advance.
situations.common_mistakes: Defense throws to first for a batter who is already out and lets the runner take extra bases; batter runs when he can't and draws a throw that helps no one.

situations.name: Dropped third strike, runner on third, 1 out
situations.offense: First base is open, so the batter can run: sprint to first the moment the ball gets away. The runner on third watches the catcher: if the catcher throws to first, that's often the chance to break for home.
situations.defense: Tag the batter if he's close, or throw to first. Before throwing, check the runner on third; the corner infielders should call it out. A rushed throw can give away the winning run.
situations.common_mistakes: Batter doesn't run because he thinks strike three ends it; runner on third doesn't read the throw; catcher throws to first without looking the runner back.

situations.name: Runner hit by a fair batted ball, bases loaded, no outs
situations.offense: One out, and the inning isn't over. A runner hit by a fair batted ball that no fielder has touched is out, and the ball is dead at that moment, even if it later rolls foul. Nothing after the dead ball counts. The batter is awarded first base and only forced runners move up one base, so with the bases loaded: the batter goes to first, the runner from first to second, the runner from second to third, and no run scores. Coaches: when you hear 'dead ball', stop calling for runners to go and let the umpires place them.
situations.defense: Once the umpire calls dead ball, tags and throws don't count, however good they were: hold the ball and let the umpires place the runners. The key judgment is whether a fielder touched the ball before it hit the runner. If she did, the ball stays live and the runner isn't out unless she interfered on purpose, so the tags that followed would count.
situations.common_mistakes: The umpire calls the runner out but doesn't kill the play loudly, so everyone keeps playing; a second umpire calls more outs on a ball that was already dead; coaches yell players into extra running and tagging; the crew changes a call because of the noise instead of getting together. Fix: 'Time! Dead ball!' with both arms up, a quick crew conference, then one calm explanation to each coach.

situations.name: Slow roller rolls foul, then back fair before first base
situations.offense: It's a fair ball, so the batter is a runner and the out at first stands. A ground ball that hasn't reached first or third base isn't foul just because it crossed the line: it's judged where it stops or where a fielder first touches it. This one rolled foul, came back, and was picked up in fair territory, so it was fair and in play. Umpires usually signal a fair ball by pointing toward fair territory without saying anything; only foul is called out loud. Batter: run on every ball you hit until you hear 'Foul!' or 'Time!'
situations.defense: Pick the ball up and make the play: step on first or throw there. A slow roller near the line that's still rolling can be left alone; if it stops or you touch it in foul territory before it reaches the base, it's foul. Fielders, like batters, play until the umpire stops it.
situations.common_mistakes: The batter stands at the plate because the ball crossed the line once; the fielder picks it up and freezes; the umpire's fair signal is late or small, so nobody sees it; coaches on both sides shout directions and the players try to learn the rule in the middle of the play. Fix: the plate umpire points fair clearly the moment the ball is touched in fair territory, and coaches teach 'run until you hear foul' at practice, not during the play.

situations.name: Two runners on the same base
situations.offense: Both runners stay on the base until the umpire rules; never step off thinking you're out. The base belongs to the lead runner unless the lead runner was forced to advance; then it belongs to the trailing runner. The runner who isn't entitled to the base looks to the coach: go back to the base they came from if it's open and they can make it.
situations.defense: Tag both runners while they're on the base. The umpire calls out the one who wasn't entitled to it, so tagging both removes the guesswork. Then look for the next play.
situations.common_mistakes: A runner walks off the base thinking the play is over and gets tagged; the fielder tags only one runner, the wrong one; the trailing runner freezes between bases instead of checking the coach.

situations.name: Fly ball with fewer than two outs
situations.offense: On a deep fly ball, go back and tag up: leave only after the catch, on the coach's call. On a shallow fly, go halfway, or as far as you can and still get back, so you can advance if it drops or return if it's caught. Never run on contact with fewer than two outs on a ball in the air.
situations.defense: Catch it, then throw ahead of the lead runner to the base they're heading for, through the cut-off. If a runner left before the catch, appeal by throwing to that base before the runner gets back.
situations.common_mistakes: Running on contact with fewer than two outs and getting doubled off; leaving the base before the catch; tagging up on a shallow fly and getting thrown out.

situations.name: Two outs: run on contact
situations.offense: With two outs, every runner runs on any batted ball. If the ball is caught the inning is over anyway, so there's nothing to protect; if it drops or gets through, runs score. Run hard and find the base coach.
situations.defense: Take the sure out. With two outs, get the force at the closest base or the out at first; don't chase the lead runner.
situations.common_mistakes: Runners waiting on a fly ball with two outs; fielders trying for a harder play instead of the easy force that ends the inning.

situations.name: Runner on second, ground ball, fewer than two outs
situations.offense: Ball hit in front of you (to the shortstop or third baseman): hold, unless you're forced. Ball hit behind you (to the right side): go to third. If first base is also occupied you're forced, so run. Line drive: freeze until it goes through.
situations.defense: Look the runner back before throwing to first. If the runner breaks for third on a ball hit in front of them, throw to third.
situations.common_mistakes: Running into an out on a ball hit to the left side; forgetting you're forced when first base is occupied; breaking on a line drive and getting doubled off.

situations.name: Rounding a base: find the base coach
situations.offense: Pick up the base coach before you reach the base. Round it hard only when the coach waves you on; stop and get back on a stop sign. When the ball is behind you, the coach makes the call; at third base the third-base coach decides whether you score.
situations.defense: Throw behind a runner who rounds too far, and hit the cut-off so trailing runners can't take an extra base.
situations.common_mistakes: Running with your head down and missing the stop sign; watching the ball instead of the coach when it's behind you; slowing down before the coach gives a sign.

stories.title: The playoff game nobody scripted
stories.text: In a do-or-die playoff game, our best pitchers weren't available, so I started a kid who hadn't had many pitching reps for us. It was a risk. He went out, threw strikes, and his pitches weren't fast and he didn't strike many kids out, but the slower speed meant fewer hard-hit balls, and the defense stepped up. That success started to feed the whole team: they hit well, ran the bases well and played an outstanding team game, because they had to. Everyone had to step up and play their part. That year they won the championship. The championship game ended on a dropped third strike with a runner on third and one out. The batter hadn't had a hit all year, not one. He'd been hit by pitches several times and was really scared at the plate. He ran, and the runner who scored from third was playing baseball for the first time. Those moments aren't scripted. They happen because kids are put in situations where they can fail or succeed.
